title: Choosing a distro
summary: Pick the right distro for servers, desktops, containers, embedded devices and Windows (WSL).

steps.title: Servers
body: For servers you want **long support, predictable updates and good documentation**:
- **Ubuntu LTS**: the most common cloud image, huge community, 5 years (10+ with Ubuntu Pro).
- **Debian stable**: conservative, community-run, about 5 years with LTS.
- **RHEL** and its rebuilds **Rocky Linux** / **AlmaLinux**: 10 years per major version, SELinux on, favoured by enterprises and certified software (databases, SAP).
- **SLES**: enterprise, strong in SAP and parts of Europe.
- **Amazon Linux 2023**: AWS-tuned, Fedora-based, fits EC2 and its tooling.
Rule of thumb: pick what your team, vendor support and monitoring already know. Changing distros later costs more than any feature difference.

steps.prompt: Match the requirement to a sensible server choice.
pairs: certified enterprise software needs RHEL compatibility, no subscription budget
most tutorials and cloud images, 5-year support
running on EC2 with AWS tools preinstalled
a community distro that changes as little as possible

steps.title: Desktops, containers, embedded, WSL
body: - **Desktops**: Ubuntu, Fedora Workstation (fresh GNOME, close to upstream), Linux Mint (familiar for Windows users), Arch or Tumbleweed for the latest everything, Pop!_OS for laptops with NVIDIA.
- **Containers**: `alpine` (tiny, musl), `debian:bookworm-slim` / `ubuntu` (glibc, familiar), Red Hat **UBI** images, or **distroless** images with only your app and its runtime (more in module 8).
- **Embedded / IoT**: Raspberry Pi OS (Debian-based), Yocto/Buildroot to build a custom minimal system, Alpine, Ubuntu Core.

- **WSL** (Windows Subsystem for Linux): WSL 2 runs a real Linux kernel in a lightweight VM on Windows. `wsl --install` gives Ubuntu by default; `wsl --list --online` shows others (Debian, openSUSE, Fedora, Alma, Kali...). Files on the Linux side (`~`) are much faster than `/mnt/c/...`.

steps.prompt: Best first pick for the job?
items: an Oracle database needing RHEL compatibility
a developer who always wants the newest compiler

steps.prompt: Your WSL build of a Node project in `/mnt/c/Users/ana/src/app` takes 3 minutes but 20 seconds in `~/src/app`. Why?
options: `/mnt/c` is the Windows file system reached across the VM boundary, so many small file operations are slow
WSL throttles the C: drive on purpose
Node is slower on NTFS by design
the Linux home is an SSD and C: is not
steps.explain: Keep projects inside the Linux file system in WSL 2, and open them from Windows with `\\wsl$` or VS Code's WSL extension.

steps.prompt: Install WSL with Debian instead of the default Ubuntu.

steps.title: Pick for the scenario
steps.prompt: A team ships a .NET API as a container. It uses a native library built against glibc, and the security team wants a small image with as few packages as possible, but the on-call engineers need a shell for debugging in staging. Which base is the best first choice?
options: `debian:trixie-slim` (or the vendor's Debian-based runtime image), with a distroless or chiseled variant for production
`archlinux`, because its packages are the newest
`ubuntu:26.04` desktop image, so the engineers feel at home
steps.explain: A glibc native library rules out Alpine (musl) without extra work. Debian slim gives glibc and a shell; for production the same app can move to a distroless or Ubuntu chiseled image with no shell at all. Rolling releases like Arch are a poor base for reproducible images, and desktop images are far too big. There is no single right distro, only one that fits the constraints you can name.
